claim: Atxn7 is a subunit of the SAGA chromatin remodeling complex.
source: Atxn7, a subunit of SAGA chromatin remodeling complex, is subject to polyglutamine expansion at the amino terminus, causing spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7), a progressive retinal and neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Polyglutamine expansion at the amino terminus of Atxn7 causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7).
source: Atxn7, a subunit of SAGA chromatin remodeling complex, is subject to polyglutamine expansion at the amino terminus, causing spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7), a progressive retinal and neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is a well-established causal relationship cited in the introduction with references.

claim: SCA7 is a progressive retinal and neurodegenerative disease.
source: Atxn7, a subunit of SAGA chromatin remodeling complex, is subject to polyglutamine expansion at the amino terminus, causing spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7), a progressive retinal and neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is a direct characterization of SCA7 disease.

claim: Within SAGA, the Atxn7 amino terminus anchors Non-stop, a deubiquitinase, to the complex.
source: Within SAGA, the Atxn7 amino terminus anchors Non-stop, a deubiquitinase, to the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Lee et al., 2009).

claim: Non-stop, dissociated from Atxn7, interacts with Arp2/3 and WAVE regulatory complexes (WRC).
source: This revealed Non-stop, dissociated from Atxn7, interacts with Arp2/3 and WAVE regulatory complexes (WRC), which control actin cytoskeleton assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Arp2/3 and WRC control actin cytoskeleton assembly.
source: This revealed Non-stop, dissociated from Atxn7, interacts with Arp2/3 and WAVE regulatory complexes (WRC), which control actin cytoskeleton assembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these complexes.

claim: Non-stop counters polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of WRC subunit SCAR.
source: There, Non-stop countered polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of WRC subunit SCAR.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 4C and 4D showing increased ubiquitination upon Non-stop knockdown and rescue by proteasome inhibition.

claim: Non-stop augmentation increases SCAR protein levels dependent on conserved WRC interacting receptor sequences (WIRS).
source: Dependent on conserved WRC interacting receptor sequences (WIRS), Non-stop augmentation increased protein levels, and directed subcellular localization, of SCAR, decreasing cell area and number of protrusions.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 6 showing that Non-stop overexpression increases SCAR levels and that WIRS mutations reduce this effect.

claim: Non-stop augmentation directs subcellular localization of SCAR dependent on conserved WIRS motifs.
source: Dependent on conserved WRC interacting receptor sequences (WIRS), Non-stop augmentation increased protein levels, and directed subcellular localization, of SCAR, decreasing cell area and number of protrusions.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A showing colocalization of Non-stop and SCAR.

claim: Non-stop augmentation decreases cell area and number of protrusions.
source: Dependent on conserved WRC interacting receptor sequences (WIRS), Non-stop augmentation increased protein levels, and directed subcellular localization, of SCAR, decreasing cell area and number of protrusions.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 5B showing reduced cell area and projections upon Non-stop overexpression.

claim: Heterozygous mutation of SCAR did not significantly rescue knockdown of Atxn7 in vivo.
source: In vivo, heterozygous mutation of SCAR did not significantly rescue knockdown of Atxn7, but heterozygous mutation of Atxn7 rescued haploinsufficiency of SCAR.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing axon targeting defects.

claim: Heterozygous mutation of Atxn7 rescued haploinsufficiency of SCAR.
source: In vivo, heterozygous mutation of SCAR did not significantly rescue knockdown of Atxn7, but heterozygous mutation of Atxn7 rescued haploinsufficiency of SCAR.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7C showing rescue of F-actin levels.

claim: SAGA is an approximately 1.8 MDa, modular, multi-protein complex.
source: The Spt Ada Gcn5 Acetyltransferase (SAGA) transcriptional coactivator complex is an approximately 1.8 MDa, modular, multi-protein complex, bearing two enzymatic subunits (Gcn5 acetyltransferase and Non-stop deubiquitinase) housed in separate modules of the complex (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAGA complex structure, supported by citation.

claim: SAGA bears two enzymatic subunits: Gcn5 acetyltransferase and Non-stop deubiquitinase.
source: The Spt Ada Gcn5 Acetyltransferase (SAGA) transcriptional coactivator complex is an approximately 1.8 MDa, modular, multi-protein complex, bearing two enzymatic subunits (Gcn5 acetyltransferase and Non-stop deubiquitinase) housed in separate modules of the complex (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAGA complex composition, supported by citation.

claim: The enzymatic subunits of SAGA are housed in separate modules of the complex.
source: The Spt Ada Gcn5 Acetyltransferase (SAGA) transcriptional coactivator complex is an approximately 1.8 MDa, modular, multi-protein complex, bearing two enzymatic subunits (Gcn5 acetyltransferase and Non-stop deubiquitinase) housed in separate modules of the complex (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAGA complex organization, supported by citation.

claim: Mutation of Atxn7 and non-stop leads to aberrant gene expression.
source: Mutation of Atxn7 and non-stop leads to aberrant gene expression, defective non-homologous end joining, decreased immune response, reduced replicative lifespan, neurodegeneration, blindness, tumorigenesis, and cancer (Glinsky et al., 2005; Weake et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2014; Lang et al., 2011; Bonnet et al., 2014; Furrer et al., 2011; Li et al., 2018; Mohan et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting these phenotypes.

claim: SCA7 is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion of the ATXN7 gene.
source: The progressive retinal and neurodegenerative disease Spinocerebellar Ataxia type 7 (SCA7) is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion of the ATXN7 gene, resulting in polyglutamine (polyQ) expansion at the amino terminus of the Atxn7 protein (Giunti et al., 1999; David et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of SCA7, supported by citations.

claim: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion results in polyglutamine expansion at the amino terminus of the Atxn7 protein.
source: The progressive retinal and neurodegenerative disease Spinocerebellar Ataxia type 7 (SCA7) is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion of the ATXN7 gene, resulting in polyglutamine (polyQ) expansion at the amino terminus of the Atxn7 protein (Giunti et al., 1999; David et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular consequence of the genetic mutation, supported by citations.

claim: SCA7 disease is characterized by progressive cone-rod dystrophy leading to blindness.
source: SCA7 disease is characterized by progressive cone-rod dystrophy leading to blindness, and progressive degeneration of the spine and cerebellum (Martin, 2012; Garden, 1993).
evidence: This is established clinical characterization of SCA7, supported by citations.

claim: SCA7 disease is characterized by progressive degeneration of the spine and cerebellum.
source: SCA7 disease is characterized by progressive cone-rod dystrophy leading to blindness, and progressive degeneration of the spine and cerebellum (Martin, 2012; Garden, 1993).
evidence: This is established clinical characterization of SCA7, supported by citations.

claim: Loss of Atxn7 in Drosophila leads to a phenotype similar to overexpression of the polyQ-expanded amino terminal truncation of human Atxn7.
source: In Drosophila, loss of Atxn7 leads to a phenotype similar to overexpression of the polyQ-expanded amino terminal truncation of human Atxn7 (Latouche et al., 2007) – reduced life span, reduced mobility, and retinal degeneration (Mohan et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of Atxn7 in Drosophila leads to reduced life span.
source: In Drosophila, loss of Atxn7 leads to a phenotype similar to overexpression of the polyQ-expanded amino terminal truncation of human Atxn7 (Latouche et al., 2007) – reduced life span, reduced mobility, and retinal degeneration (Mohan et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of Atxn7 in Drosophila leads to reduced mobility.

claim: Loss of Atxn7 in Drosophila leads to retinal degeneration.

claim: Without Atxn7, the Drosophila DUBm is released, enzymatically active, from SAGA.
source: Without Atxn7, the Drosophila DUBm is released, enzymatically active, from SAGA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Mohan et al., 2014a).

claim: Once released, the DUBm acts as a gain-of-function, leading to reduced ubiquitination of H2B.
source: Once released, the module acts as a gain-of-function, leading to reduced ubiquitination of H2B.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Mohan et al., 2014a).

claim: The mammalian DUBm binds and deubiquitinates substrates without Atxn7 in vitro, albeit at a lower rate.
source: Similarly, the mammalian DUBm binds and deubiquitinates substrates without Atxn7 in vitro, albeit at a lower rate (Lan et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Reducing non-stop copy number alleviates lethality associated with loss of Atxn7.
source: Consistent with Non-stop release and over activity mediating the Drosophila Atxn7 loss-of-function phenotype, reducing non-stop copy number alleviates lethality associated with loss of Atxn7 (Mohan et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Non-stop is a critical mediator of retinal axon guidance.
source: Non-stop is a critical mediator of retinal axon guidance and important for glial cell survival (Weake et al., 2008; Martin et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Non-stop is important for glial cell survival.
source: Non-stop is a critical mediator of retinal axon guidance and important for glial cell survival (Weake et al., 2008; Martin et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Abnormal ubiquitin signaling in the nervous system contributes to a number of genetic and spontaneous neurological and retinal diseases.
source: Interestingly, abnormal ubiquitin signaling in the nervous system contributes to a number of genetic and spontaneous neurological and retinal diseases, including SCA3, SCAR16, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, and Huntington's disease (Petrucelli and Dawson, 2004; Campello et al., 2013; Mohan et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The DUBm deubiquitinates H2Bub.
source: Few functions are known for the DUBm beyond deubiquitination of H2Bub, H2Aub, shelterin, and FBP1 (Atanassov and Dent, 2011; Atanassov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The DUBm deubiquitinates H2Aub.

claim: Both increased and decreased H2Bub have been shown to hinder gene expression.
source: Interestingly, both increased and decreased H2Bub have been shown to hinder gene expression, and imbalances (whether up or down) in ubiquitination are observed in retinal and neurological diseases (Ristic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Imbalances in ubiquitination are observed in retinal and neurological diseases.

claim: Non-stop-containing complexes were purified from nuclear extracts via tandem affinity purification.
source: Non-stop-containing protein complexes were purified from nuclear extracts via tandem affinity purification of their epitope tags: FLAG, then HA (Suganuma et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Non-stop-containing complexes are unique compared to Atxn7 and WDA purifications.
source: Although similar in profile to Atxn7 and WDA purifications, Non-stop-containing complexes were unique, indicating Non-stop has novel interaction partners.
evidence: This is based on comparison of silver stain profiles shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Non-stop has novel interaction partners.
source: Although similar in profile to Atxn7 and WDA purifications, Non-stop-containing complexes were unique, indicating Non-stop has novel interaction partners.
evidence: This is inferred from the unique profile of Non-stop purifications.

claim: Non-stop elutes in additional fractions beyond those containing SAGA.
source: Atxn7 and Ada2b are SAGA-specific subunits. Their elution from the gel-filtration column indicates those fractions contain SAGA (Mohan et al., 2014a; Kusch et al., 2003). Non-stop eluted in additional fractions (Figure 1E, upper).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E comparing elution profiles of Atxn7, Ada2b, and Non-stop.

claim: In Non-stop purifications, deubiquitinase activity resolved into three major peaks.
source: In Non-stop purifications, however, deubiquitinase activity resolved into three major peaks.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E lower panel using ubiquitin-AMC assay.

claim: Peak deubiquitinase activity in Atxn7 complexes was detected around 1.8MDa, consistent with SAGA complex.
source: In complexes purified through Atxn7, peak deubiquitinase activity was detected around 1.8MDa, consistent with SAGA complex and previous purification, fractionation, and mass spectrometry of Atxn7, which is reproduced here for purposes of comparison (Mohan et al., 2014a; Kusch et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic activity assay data and supported by citations.

claim: Group 1 contained SAGA complex subunits from each of the major (HAT/TAF/SPT/DUB) modules.
source: Consistent with previous characterizations of SAGA, Group 1 contained SAGA complex subunits from each of the major (HAT/TAF/SPT/DUB) modules (Mohan et al., 2014a; Kusch et al., 2003; ; Lee et al., 2011; Setiaputra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Group 2 contained the DUBm: Non-stop, Sgf11, and E(y)2.
source: Group 2 contained the DUBm: Non-stop, Sgf11, and E(y)2 – indicating the DUBm remained intact during purification and fractionation (Köhler et al., 2010; Samara et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The DUBm remained intact during purification and fractionation.
source: Group 2 contained the DUBm: Non-stop, Sgf11, and E(y)2 – indicating the DUBm remained intact during purification and fractionation (Köhler et al., 2010; Samara et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-purification of all three DUBm components.

claim: Histone H2A and H2B were detected in Group 2.
source: Histone H2A and H2B were also detected in Group 2, suggesting the DUBm co-purified with known substrates, further confirming conditions were suitable for preservation and identification of endogenous interactions (Figure 2A) (Zhao et al., 2008; Henry et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A mass spectrometry data.

claim: The DUBm co-purified with known substrates (H2A and H2B).
source: Histone H2A and H2B were also detected in Group 2, suggesting the DUBm co-purified with known substrates, further confirming conditions were suitable for preservation and identification of endogenous interactions (Figure 2A) (Zhao et al., 2008; Henry et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of H2A and H2B in the purification, supported by citations.

claim: Arp2/3 complex (all subunits) were represented in high ratio to DUBm members in Group 2.
source: Notably, within Group 2, Arp2/3 complex (all subunits) and WRC subunits SCAR, Hem, and Sra-1 were represented in high ratio to DUBm members, as determined by dNSAF (Figure 2A) (Pollard and Beltzner, 2002; Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A mass spectrometry data.

claim: WRC subunits SCAR, Hem, and Sra-1 were represented in high ratio to DUBm members in Group 2.
source: Notably, within Group 2, Arp2/3 complex (all subunits) and WRC subunits SCAR, Hem, and Sra-1 were represented in high ratio to DUBm members, as determined by dNSAF (Figure 2A) (Pollard and Beltzner, 2002; Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A mass spectrometry data.

source: WRC complex activates Arp2/3 to promote actin branching, which is important for a range of cellular activities including cell migration, cell adhesion, exocytosis, endocytosis, maintenance of nuclear shape, and phagocytosis (Zallen et al., 2002; Takenawa and Miki, 2001; Alekhina et al., 2017; Navarro-Lérida et al., 2015; Vishavkarma et al., 2014; Verboon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SCAR is particularly important for cytoplasmic organization in the blastoderm.
source: In Drosophila, SCAR is particularly important for cytoplasmic organization in the blastoderm, for egg chamber structure during oogenesis, axon development in the central nervous system, and adult eye morphology (Zallen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SCAR is particularly important for egg chamber structure during oogenesis.
source: In Drosophila, SCAR is particularly important for cytoplasmic organization in the blastoderm, for egg chamber structure during oogenesis, axon development in the central nervous system, and adult eye morphology (Zallen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SCAR is particularly important for axon development in the central nervous system.
source: In Drosophila, SCAR is particularly important for cytoplasmic organization in the blastoderm, for egg chamber structure during oogenesis, axon development in the central nervous system, and adult eye morphology (Zallen et al., 2002).

claim: SCAR is particularly important for adult eye morphology.
source: In Drosophila, SCAR is particularly important for cytoplasmic organization in the blastoderm, for egg chamber structure during oogenesis, axon development in the central nervous system, and adult eye morphology (Zallen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SCAR-FH associates with endogenous Non-stop.
source: Reciprocal immunoprecipitation of SCAR-FH utilizing an anti-FLAG resin followed by immunoblotting for Non-stop using an anti-Non-stop antibody confirmed SCAR-FH associated with endogenous Non-stop (Figure 2C) (Mohan et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C by reciprocal immunoprecipitation.

claim: Non-stop localized similarly to SCAR, but also further within nuclei.
source: Non-stop localized similarly to SCAR, but also further within nuclei.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D by immunofluorescence.

claim: Non-stop overlaps with portions of F-actin.
source: Examination of the spatial relationship between Non-stop and F-actin, using phalloidin, revealed Non-stop overlapping with portions of F-actin/phalloidin (Figure 2E) (Cooper, 1987).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E by immunofluorescence.

claim: In Atxn7 mutant extracts, approximately 1.4 times more SCAR was present per Non-stop captured.
source: In Atxn7 mutant extracts, approximately 1.4 times more SCAR was present per Non-stop captured (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A by endogenous immunoprecipitation and quantification.

claim: Atxn7 retains a pool of Non-stop that can be freed to interact with SCAR.
source: This suggests Atxn7 retains a pool of Non-stop that can be freed to interact with SCAR.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased Non-stop-SCAR interaction in Atxn7 mutants.

claim: Cells treated with Non-stop-targeting RNAs showed approximately 70% decrease in SCAR protein levels relative to LacZ control knock-down.
source: Protein extracts from Non-stop knockdown cells consistently showed approximately 70% decrease in SCAR protein levels relative to LacZ control knock-down.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B by immunoblotting after RNAi treatment.

claim: Cells treated with Atxn7-targeting RNAs showed 2.5-fold increase in SCAR protein.
source: Consistent with a model in which Atxn7 restrains Non-stop deubiquitinase activity, cells treated with Atxn7-targeting RNAs showed 2.5-fold increase in SCAR protein (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B by immunoblotting after RNAi treatment.

claim: Larval brain extracts from Atxn7 mutants showed about 2.5-fold increase in SCAR protein levels.
source: Larval brain extracts from Atxn7 mutants showed about 2.5-fold increase in SCAR protein levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C by immunoblotting of larval brain extracts.

claim: In non-stop mutant extracts SCAR was decreased approximately 75%.
source: In non-stop mutant extracts SCAR was decreased approximately 75% (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C by immunoblotting of larval brain extracts.

claim: In genome wide analysis of glial nuclei isolated from mutant larvae, SCAR transcript was significantly down regulated by one fold in Non-stop deficient glia.
source: In genome wide analysis of glial nuclei isolated from mutant larvae, SCAR transcript was significantly down regulated by one fold in Non-stop deficient glia, but not in Sgf11 deficient glia (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on published genome-wide analysis data, supported by citation.

claim: SCAR transcript was not significantly down regulated in Sgf11 deficient glia.
source: In genome wide analysis of glial nuclei isolated from mutant larvae, SCAR transcript was significantly down regulated by one fold in Non-stop deficient glia, but not in Sgf11 deficient glia (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on published genome-wide analysis data, supported by citation.

claim: Non-stop knockdown showed a one half decrease in SCAR transcript levels.
source: To confirm the relationship between Non-stop and SCAR gene expression, we used qRT-PCR to measure SCAR transcript levels in BG3 cells knocked-down for non-stop. We found a similar one half decrease in SCAR transcript levels (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D by qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Examination of Atxn7 knockdown showed no decrease in SCAR transcript levels.
source: However, examination of Atxn7 knockdown showed no decrease in SCAR transcript levels (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D by qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: SCAR gene expression is independent of Atxn7 or Sgf11.
source: Therefore, while non-stop loss leads to modest decreases in SCAR transcripts, SCAR gene expression is independent of Atxn7 or Sgf11, suggesting this gene is not SAGA-dependent or dependent on Non-stop enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Atxn7 knockdown does not affect SCAR transcript levels and Sgf11 mutants do not show SCAR transcript changes.

claim: Heterozygous SCAR brains produced 40% less SCAR transcript than wild-type brains.
source: qRT-PCR analysis showed heterozygous SCAR brains produced 40% less SCAR transcript than wild-type brains (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E by qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Heterozygous SCAR mutant and wild-type brains showed similar amounts of SCAR protein.
source: However, heterozygous SCAR mutant and wild-type brains showed similar amounts of SCAR protein, demonstrating this amount of transcript is sufficient for full protein production (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F by immunoblotting.

claim: In Drosophila, HEM, SRA-1, and Abi recruit an unidentified deubiquitinase to balance SCAR regulation through a constant ubiquitination-proteasomal degradation mechanism.
source: In Drosophila, HEM, SRA-1, and Abi recruit an unidentified deubiquitinase to balance SCAR regulation through a constant ubiquitination-proteasomal degradation mechanism facilitating rapid changes in SCAR protein amount and localization (Chen et al., 2014; Kunda et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mammals, the USP7 deubiquitinase acts as a molecular rheostat controlling proteasomal degradation of WASH.
source: In mammals, the USP7 deubiquitinase acts as a molecular rheostat controlling proteasomal degradation of WASH (Hao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Non-stop(C406A) bound to SCAR approximately 4-fold more than wild-type Non-stop.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that Non-stop(C406A) bound to SCAR approximately 4-fold more than wild-type Non-stop while Non-stop(C406S) bound only about 1/3rd as well (Figure 4A and B, upper panels).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting.

claim: Non-stop(C406S) bound to SCAR only about 1/3rd as well as wild-type Non-stop.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that Non-stop(C406A) bound to SCAR approximately 4-fold more than wild-type Non-stop while Non-stop(C406S) bound only about 1/3rd as well (Figure 4A and B, upper panels).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting.

claim: Both Non-stop(C406A) and Non-stop(C406S) mutants incorporated into SAGA.
source: To verify both mutants incorporated into SAGA, interaction with Ada2b was confirmed (Figure 4A and B, lower panels).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4A and 4B by immunoblotting for Ada2b.

claim: Knock-down of Non-stop nearly tripled levels of SCAR polyubiquitination.
source: Immunoprecipitation of SCAR followed by immunoblotting with a ubiquitin-specific antibody revealed that knock-down of Non-stop nearly tripled levels of SCAR polyubiquitination (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting for ubiquitin.

claim: Treating non-stop brains with MG132 rescued SCAR protein amounts to levels found in wild type brains.
source: Treating non-stop brains with MG132 rescued SCAR protein amounts to levels found in wild type brains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D by ex vivo brain culture with proteasome inhibitor.

claim: Upon expression of Non-stop-FH in BG3 cells, endogenous SCAR protein levels increased five-fold compared with mock transfected cells.
source: Upon expression of Non-stop-FH in BG3 cells, endogenous SCAR protein levels increased five-fold compared with mock transfected cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A by immunofluorescence and quantification.

claim: Increased SCAR protein co-compartmentalized with Non-stop, even within the nucleus.
source: Increased SCAR protein co-compartmentalized with Non-stop, even within the nucleus, where SCAR function is more enigmatic (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A by immunofluorescence.

claim: As the amount of Non-stop in the nucleus increased, so did the amount of SCAR in the nucleus.
source: As the amount of Non-stop in the nucleus increased, so did the amount of SCAR in the nucleus, showing Non-stop was driving SCAR localization (R2 = 0.8) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A by correlation analysis of nuclear:cytoplasmic ratios.

claim: Cells overexpressing Non-stop displayed fewer projections and covered less total area.
source: Using phalloidin to observe F-actin in cells overexpressing Non-stop, a substantial change in cell morphology was observed. Cells displayed fewer projections and covered less total area (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: Overexpression of SCAR alone led to reductions in cell area and number of projections observed.
source: Overexpression of SCAR alone similarly led to reductions in cell area and number of projections observed (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: Primary sequence analysis of DUBm subunits revealed four WIRS-conforming sequences on Non-stop.
source: Primary sequence analysis of DUBm subunits revealed four WIRS-conforming sequences on Non-stop and three on mammalian Non-stop orthologue USP22.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Primary sequence analysis revealed three WIRS-conforming sequences on mammalian Non-stop orthologue USP22.
source: Primary sequence analysis of DUBm subunits revealed four WIRS-conforming sequences on Non-stop and three on mammalian Non-stop orthologue USP22.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: WIRS1 and 3 are conserved in location between Drosophila and mammalian Non-stop.
source: These were numbered from 0 to 3, with WIRS1 and 3 conserved in location between Drosophila and mammalian Non-stop. (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A by sequence alignment.

claim: None of the other DUBm components bore conserved WIRS motifs.
source: None of the other DUBm components bore conserved WIRS motifs.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Non-stop WIRS mutant displayed an approximate 80% reduction in SCAR binding.
source: This mutant displayed an approximate 80% reduction in SCAR binding, but still integrated into SAGA as observed by maintenance of Atxn7 binding (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting.

claim: Non-stop WIRS mutant still integrated into SAGA as observed by maintenance of Atxn7 binding.
source: This mutant displayed an approximate 80% reduction in SCAR binding, but still integrated into SAGA as observed by maintenance of Atxn7 binding (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting for Atxn7.

claim: Each Non-stop WIRS mutant produced less SCAR protein than wild type.
source: In each case, the Non-stop mutant produced less SCAR protein than wild type, suggesting that these motifs are indeed important for Non-stop mediated increases in SCAR protein levels (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C by immunofluorescence and quantification.

claim: Mutant Non-stop was less potent for decreasing cell area and decreasing the number of cell protrusions.
source: Mutant Non-stop was also less potent for decreasing cell area and decreasing the number of cell protrusions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: The effect of mutating each WIRS was not equivalent, suggesting a hierarchy for which is most important for WRC stabilization.
source: The effect of mutating each WIRS was not equivalent, suggesting a hierarchy for which is most important for WRC stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of individual WIRS mutations shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: In Non-stop mutants, F-actin intensity was reduced by approximately 70%.
source: In Non-stop mutants, F-actin intensity was reduced by approximately 70% (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: In Atxn7 mutants, F-actin levels increased approximately 1.7 times.
source: In Atxn7 mutants, F-actin levels increased approximately 1.7 times (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: In Atxn7 heterozygotes, F-actin levels were not significantly different than wild-type.
source: In Atxn7 heterozygotes, F-actin levels were not significantly different than wild-type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: In SCAR heterozygotes, F-actin levels were decreased.
source: In SCAR heterozygotes, however, F-actin levels were decreased.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: Combining Atxn7 and SCAR heterozygous mutants rescued F-actin levels.
source: Combining Atxn7 and SCAR heterozygous mutants rescued F-actin levels.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C by phalloidin staining and quantification.

claim: Neural-specific expression of Atxn7 RNAi results in defective axon targeting.
source: Neural-specific expression of Atxn7 RNAi (Dietzl et al., 2007), driven by elav-Gal4, results in defective axon targeting.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 by Chaoptin staining.

claim: Knockdown of Non-stop led to defective axon targeting.
source: Similarly, knockdown of either Non-stop (Perkins et al., 2015) or SCAR (Perkins et al., 2015) led to defective axon targeting.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 by Chaoptin staining and supported by citation.

claim: Knockdown of SCAR led to defective axon targeting.
source: Similarly, knockdown of either Non-stop (Perkins et al., 2015) or SCAR (Perkins et al., 2015) led to defective axon targeting.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 by Chaoptin staining and supported by citation.

claim: Gcn5 knock-down resulted in wild-type axon targeting.
source: Gcn5 knock-down (Dietzl et al., 2007), however, resulted in wild-type axon targeting.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 by Chaoptin staining.

claim: Atxn7 knockdown in a SCAR heterozygous background showed fewer defects in axon targeting (62% normal vs 52% normal), but this difference was not sufficient to achieve statistical significance (p=0.73).
source: Although there were fewer defects in axon targeting (62% normal vs 52% normal), this difference was not sufficient to achieve statistical significance (p=0.73).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 by Chaoptin staining and statistical analysis.

claim: Purification of Atxn7-containing complexes indicated that Atxn7 functions predominantly as a member of SAGA.
source: Purification of Atxn7-containing complexes indicated that Atxn7 functions predominantly as a member of SAGA (Mohan et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In yeast, the Atxn7 orthologue, Sgf73, can be separated from SAGA along with the deubiquitinase module by the proteasome regulatory particle.
source: In yeast, the Atxn7 orthologue, Sgf73, can be separated from SAGA along with the deubiquitinase module by the proteasome regulatory particle (Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Without Sgf73, the yeast deubiquitinase module is inactive.
source: Without Sgf73, the yeast deubiquitinase module is inactive (Samara et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In higher eukaryotes, Atxn7 increases, but is not necessary for Non-stop/USP22 enzymatic activity in vitro.
source: In higher eukaryotes, Atxn7 increases, but is not necessary for Non-stop/USP22 enzymatic activity in vitro (Mohan et al., 2014a; Lan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SCAR was previously described to be regulated by a constant ubiquitination/deubiquitination mechanism.
source: SCAR was previously described to be regulated by a constant ubiquitination/deubiquitination mechanism (Kunda et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Nuclear Arp2/3 and WRC have been linked to nuclear reprogramming during early development.
source: Nuclear Arp2/3 and WRC have been linked to nuclear reprogramming during early development, immune system function, and general regulation of gene expression (Yoo et al., 2007; Miyamoto et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear Arp2/3 and WRC have been linked to immune system function.
source: Nuclear Arp2/3 and WRC have been linked to nuclear reprogramming during early development, immune system function, and general regulation of gene expression (Yoo et al., 2007; Miyamoto et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear Arp2/3 and WRC have been linked to general regulation of gene expression.
source: Nuclear Arp2/3 and WRC have been linked to nuclear reprogramming during early development, immune system function, and general regulation of gene expression (Yoo et al., 2007; Miyamoto et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Distortions of nuclear shape alter chromatin domain location within the nucleus, resulting in changes in gene expression.
source: Distortions of nuclear shape alter chromatin domain location within the nucleus, resulting in changes in gene expression (Navarro-Lérida et al., 2015; Rodriguez-Mesa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear pore stability is compromised in SAGA DUBm mutants, resulting in deficient mRNA export.
source: Nuclear pore stability is compromised in SAGA DUBm mutants, resulting in deficient mRNA export (Köhler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mutants of F-actin regulatory proteins, such as Wash, show nuclear pore loss.
source: Similarly, mutants of F-actin regulatory proteins, such as Wash, show nuclear pore loss (Verboon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In yeast, the proteasome regulatory particle removes the DUBm from SAGA.
source: In yeast, the proteasome regulatory particle removes the DUBm from SAGA (Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In higher eukaryotes, caspase-7 cleaves Atxn7 at residues which would be expected to release the DUBm.
source: In higher eukaryotes, caspase-7 cleaves Atxn7 at residues which would be expected to release the DUBm, although this remains to be shown explicitly (Young et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work, but noted as not yet explicitly demonstrated.

claim: The cell maintains a pool of Non-stop that can be made available to act distally from the larger SAGA complex to modulate SCAR protein levels.
source: Overall, these findings suggest that the cell maintains a pool of Non-stop that can be made available to act distally from the larger SAGA complex to modulate SCAR protein levels (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings presented in the study.
